candidate.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — surgical-smoke engineering control and occupational exposure prevention
candidate.educational_objective: Use local surgical-smoke evacuation during electrosurgical plume generation to capture hazardous airborne contaminants close to their source before they disperse into the room.

options.A: To replace the need for general room ventilation during electrosurgery.
options.B: To remove surgical smoke only after it has dispersed into the room air.
options.C: To capture hazardous airborne contaminants close to their source before they disperse.
options.D: To prevent the electrosurgical unit from interfering with physiologic monitoring equipment.

candidate.rationale: NIOSH states that electrosurgical smoke can contain toxic gases and vapors, bioaerosols, cellular material, and viruses. General room ventilation alone is not sufficient to capture contaminants generated at the source; local exhaust ventilation such as a smoke evacuator is used to control the plume close to the surgical site, and the evacuator should be activated whenever airborne particles are produced. Therefore C is correct. A incorrectly treats local evacuation as a replacement for general ventilation, B waits until contaminants have dispersed rather than capturing them at the source, and D describes a purpose unrelated to surgical-smoke control.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Local surgical-smoke evacuation is an engineering control used to capture hazardous airborne contaminants close to the source and should be active whenever surgical procedures generate airborne particles.
candidate.source_document_title: NIOSH Hazard Controls HC11 — Control of Smoke from Laser/Electric Surgical Procedures
candidate.source_locator: CDC Stacks record description, corresponding to HC11 Hazard/Controls sections: surgical smoke may contain toxic gases and vapors, bioaerosols, cellular material, and viruses; general room ventilation is insufficient; local smoke evacuation captures contaminants near the source; the evacuator should be activated whenever airborne particles are produced. Currentness cross-check: NIOSH Healthcare Respiratory Protection > Surgical smoke (Jan. 15, 2025) directs use of control methods such as ventilation and links this NIOSH publication.

candidate.stem: During electrosurgery, why should local surgical-smoke evacuation remain active whenever smoke is produced?
